# Military medicine

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Basics of surgery > Military medicine*

[Original Article Link](/library/Os0IEh)

---

## Summary

Military medicine includes clinical medicine, i.e., health care provided to service members and their families corresponding to civilian health care services, and operational medicine, i.e., health care for service members on deployment in theaters of operation. The <u>Military Health System</u> (<u>MHS</u>) represents the cornerstone of clinical military medicine. It is designed to ensure that all active duty and reserve component personnel stay healthy and operational and that <u>health care providers</u> are properly trained to support the operational forces. Key elements of the <u>MHS</u> include <u>TRICARE</u> (a health care program designed to provide integrated health care through military treatment facilities [MTF] and civilian providers to eligible beneficiaries), expeditionary care, a <u>joint</u> staff <u>surgeon</u>, the <u>Defense Health Agency</u>, and the Uniformed Services University of Health Sciences. Combat injuries are treated according to the <u>Tactical Combat Casualty Care</u> (<u>TCCC</u>) protocol developed to reduce preventable deaths during tactical operations by increasing the <u>probability</u> of casualties reaching an MTF. <u>TCCC</u> involves 3 consecutive phases: care under fire (CUF), tactical field care (TFC), and tactical evacuation care (<u>TEC</u>). CUF mainly involves first response, especially stopping <u>massive hemorrhage</u>, returning fire, taking cover, and initiating the treatment of casualties. The TFC phase focuses on the treatment of casualties according to the <u>MARCH</u> acronym (Massive hemorrhage, Airway management, Respiration, Circulation, Head injury). Additional measures at a Casualty Collection Point (CCP) should be considered according to the PAWS acronym (Pain management, Antibiotics, Wound management, Splinting). The most common types of combat injuries are <u>blast injuries</u>, <u>stab wounds</u>, <u>burns</u>, and chemical injuries (e.g., <u>nerve gas</u> <u>poisoning</u>). Associated psychiatric conditions such as <u>posttraumatic stress disorder</u> (<u>PTSD</u>) are often chronic, requiring treatment long after deployment.

## Health care in the military

### Definitions




* Active duty service member: an individual who is available for duty full-time (i.e., 24 hours per day, 7 days a week, excluding authorized leave) in the armed forces (i.e., Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and Space Force)

* Veteran: an individual who served in the armed forces and was not dishonorably discharged

* Reserve: an individual who provides supplementary support to active duty forces when required

* Active duty retirement (retiree): a member of the military with ≥ 20 years of active service





### Military Health System (<u>MHS</u>) [[2]](/library/0AceRU0)




* Overview

* The <u>Military Health System</u> (<u>MHS</u>) is a federal health care program run by the United States Department of Defense (DOD).

* The <u>MHS</u> is led by the office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Health Affairs under the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness.

* Objectives

* Ensuring that all active duty;   and reserve component personnel;    stay healthy and operational

* Ensuring that active and reserve <u>health care providers</u> are well-trained and capable of supporting operational forces

* Providing medical benefits (e.g., coverage of prescription drug costs, surgical procedures, and check-ups) to active duty personnel and military retirees (including their families)

* Key elements [[3]](/library/ZAcZRU0)

* TRICARE

* A health care program designed to provide integrated health care through military treatment facilities and civilian providers to eligible beneficiaries, i.e., sponsors (e.g., active, reserve, and retired members of the armed forces) and their family members (i.e., spouses and children who are registered in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System)

* Approx. 9.6 million individuals receive benefits from the <u>MHS</u>.  [[4]](/library/zycr3U0)

* Individuals covered under <u>TRICARE</u>

* Active duty service members

* Dependents of active duty family service members

* National Guard and Reserve members and their dependents

* Retirees and their dependents

* Survivors

* Former spouses (subject to certain requirements)

* <u>TRICARE</u> offers different health <u>care plans</u> and benefits depending on various factors such as service status, residence, and duration of service.

* Services and supplies that are considered nonessential for the treatment of a covered condition as well as those related to a noncovered condition or treatment, are excluded, e.g: [[5]](/library/-ycD3U0)

* <u>Acupuncture</u>

* Homeopathic and herbal drugs, naturopathic care

* <u>Dyslexia</u> treatment

* Expeditionary care

* A staff of medical professionals that ensures that the operational forces are healthy and ready to deploy

* Designated medical professionals (e.g., combat medics) accompany the operational forces to provide help during battle

* Military treatment facilities (MTF): 55 full-service hospitals and more than 370 clinics on military bases around the world

* Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences

* Federal professions academy

* No tuition, but graduates are obligated to serve

* Emphasis on military health care and leadership

* <u>Joint</u> staff <u>surgeon</u>: chief medical advisor tasked with the coordination of all necessary health service-related issues (e.g., force health protection, operational medicine)

* Defense Health Agency

* A combat support agency established in 2013 to provide integrated and efficient health services to the military

* Services include developing health information technology systems, providing pharmacy and medical logistics, performing medical research, and operating <u>TRICARE</u> health benefits

* Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Health Affairs: responsible for all DOD health and force health protection policies, programs, and activities





### Transitional period programs [[6]](/library/mB1VYj0)




* Overview

* Active duty service members who separate from the military (i.e., leaving active duty before retiring) and their dependents are eligible for temporary health coverage to help with the transition to VA health or civilian health plans.

* Members who retire from active duty (i.e., ≥ 20 years of service) will be disenrolled from <u>TRICARE</u> and must enroll in a new <u>TRICARE program</u> within 90 days of retirement.

* Transitional Assistance Management Program (TAMP)

* 180 days of benefits after regular <u>TRICARE</u> benefits end

* Eligible members and their dependents can use one health plan option (e.g., a specific <u>TRICARE</u> plan, US Family Health Plan) and military medical facilities.

* No premiums

* Continued Health Care Benefit Program (CHCBP)

* 18–36 months of coverage after <u>TRICARE</u> benefits end

* Provides minimum essential coverage

* Premium-based





### Veterans Health Administration (<u>VHA</u>) [[7]](/library/_yc53U0)




* Overview

* A nationalized healthcare program funded by the United States Department of Veterans Affairs (VA)

* Led by the Under Secretary of the Veterans Affairs for Health

* America's largest integrated <u>health care system</u>

* Provides care to 9 million veterans annually

* Unlike <u>MHS</u> facilities, all <u>VHA</u> <u>health care facilities</u> are government-owned and operated.

* About 60% of all medical residents receive a part of their training in a VA hospital and/or medical research program.

* Facilities

* VA medical centers

* Outpatient clinics

* Community-based outpatient clinics

* VA community living centers

## Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC)

Trauma care guidelines are used during combat and established in three phases. The aim is to reduce preventable deaths in military personnel during tactical operations by implementing measures that increase the <u>probability</u> of a wounded soldier reaching an MTF.




### Phase 1: care under fire (CUF)




Actions taken during tactical engagement under fire:



1. * Application of precise suppression fire by all personnel (incl. casualties, if capable)
2. * Continue tactical mission
3. * Take cover
4. * Treat casualties

* Control hemorrhage

* Massive extremity hemorrhage: apply combat <u>tourniquet</u>




### Phase 2: tactical field care (TFC)




Actions taken when no longer under fire:



1. * Disarm casualties with <u>altered mental status</u> or if receiving <u>ketamine</u> or <u>fentanyl</u>
2. * First responders should follow the order of treatment itemized by the <u>MARCH</u> acronym:

* Massive hemorrhage

* Reassess any hemorrhage and control all sources of massive extremity bleeding using a <u>tourniquet</u>.

* Dress nonmassive hemorrhages with combat gauze.

* Airway management: Assess <u>airway</u> patency; insert <u>nasopharyngeal airway</u> (<u>NPA</u>) or perform <u>surgical cricothyroidotomy</u>, if necessary.

* Respiration: Insert a vented chest seal in case of open chest wounds, decompress a suspected <u>tension pneumothorax</u>, and consider ventilation/<u>oxygen therapy</u>.

* Circulation: Establish IV or <u>IO access</u> when <u>fluid resuscitation</u> and/or IV drug administration is required.

* Head injury/<u>hypothermia</u> prevention: Assess for <u>concussion</u>, remove wet clothes, and apply a ready-heat blanket.
3. * Additional measures should be considered at the Casualty Collection Point (CCP) according to the PAWS acronym:

* Pain management: Administer <u>analgesics</u>.

* Antibiotics: 1 g IV <u>ertapenem</u> or 2 g IV <u>cefotetan</u> or 400 mg oral <u>moxifloxacin</u>

* Wound management: Address <u>open wounds</u>, <u>burns</u>, and <u>open fractures</u>.

* Splinting: Stabilize <u>pelvic fractures</u> and shield <u>eye</u> injuries.




### Phase 3: tactical evacuation care (<u>TEC</u>)




* Medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) and casualty evacuation (CASEVAC) via dedicated air and/or ground vehicles to the nearest MTF.

* Continue interventions initiated during the evacuation or at the MTF.

* Assess for and document additional life-threatening injuries, <u>pain control</u>, <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, and appropriate therapy.

### Chemical injuries




#### Gulf War illness (<u>GWI</u>) [[10]](/library/RAcljU0)




* Definition: a chronic, multisystem condition seen in veterans of the 1991 Gulf War

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Estimated to affect between 175,000 and 250,000 soldiers

* More commonly seen in Army and Marine Corps veterans than in Navy or Air Force veterans

* Of the 28 coalition forces, 27 reported cases of <u>GWI</u> in their troops.

* Etiology

* Not fully understood; exposure to multiple agents is likely

* <u>GWI</u> has been linked to a variety of exposures, including:

* Fumes from destroyed chemical warfare agents (<u>sarin</u>, cyclosarin, <u>mustard gas</u>, soman)

* Pesticides (e.g., chlorpyrifos, <u>permethrin</u>, N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide)

* <u>Pyridostigmine</u> bromide

* Other chemicals (e.g., fuels, cleaners, lubricants, fumes from oil well fires)

* Multiple <u>vaccinations</u> (including <u>anthrax</u>)

* Heat

* Psychological <u>stress</u>

* Clinical features

* Chronic fatigue

* Muscle and <u>joint</u> <u>pain</u>

* Neurological deficits (e.g., <u>memory</u> impairment)

* Functional gastrointestinal problems (e.g., <u>diarrhea</u>)

* <u>Skin</u> rashes

* Diagnostics

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* <u>MRI</u> may show reductions of gray and <u>white matter</u> and increased axial diffusivity.

* Neurocognitive testing usually reveals deficits in <u>short-term memory</u>, fine motor coordination and speed, <u>executive functions</u>, and visuospatial abilities.

* Management

* No standard treatment

* <u>Coenzyme Q<sub>10</sub></u> supplementation, <u>acupuncture</u>, and <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> have proven beneficial.

* Prognosis: poor; only a few affected individuals experience substantial improvement or recovery over time





#### <u>Nerve gas</u> <u>poisoning</u> (e.g., <u>sarin</u>)



* See “<u>Sarin</u>” for details.




#### <u>Poisoning</u> with hydrocarbons



* See “<u>Hydrocarbon toxicity</u>” for details.




### Combat- and deployment-associated psychiatric conditions




* <u>Acute stress disorder</u>

* <u>Post-traumatic stress disorder</u> (<u>PTSD</u>)

* <u>Adjustment disorder</u>

## Blast injuries

<u>Blast injuries</u> frequently result in complex trauma involving both conspicuous external injuries and internal trauma induced by <u>blast waves</u> (<u>primary blast injuries</u>), which may not be immediately apparent. [[11]](/library/fv1kzi0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Account for the majority of military combat wounds; also common in civilian mass casualty events

* Associated with high rates of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality





### Etiology [[12]](/library/hv1c-i0)[[13]](/library/REblvv)




* <u>High-order explosives</u>

* Examples: TNT, <u>nitroglycerine</u>, dynamite

* Produce an explosion with a <u>supersonic overpressure wave</u> (blast wave)

* Low-order explosives

* Examples: pipe bombs, gunpowder, petrol bombs

* Produce a subsonic explosion (no <u>blast wave</u>)

* High-order and low-order explosives that produce a <u>blast wind</u> can cause additional injuries (e.g., incineration of flammable material).





### Classification




| <br>Overview of blast injuries [[11]](/library/fv1kzi0)[[13]](/library/REblvv)[[14]](/library/gv1Fzi0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Class | Mechanism | Common injuries |
| Primary blast injury | <br><br>* <u>Blast wave</u>-induced barotrauma and tissue damage (typically due to detonation of a <u>high-order explosive</u>)  [[12]](/library/hv1c-i0)<br><br>* Usually occurs in confined spaces, near walls, or within meters of the explosion  [[13]](/library/REblvv)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Blast-induced otologic injury</u>, e.g., <u>tympanic membrane rupture</u><br><br>* <u>Blast lung syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Blast-induced neurotrauma</u><br><br>* <u>Blast-induced ocular trauma</u><br><br>* <u>Blast-induced abdominal injury</u><br><br>* <u>Cardiovascular primary blast injuries</u><br><br><br> |
| Secondary blast injury | <br><br>* Blunt and/or <u>penetrating trauma</u> caused by explosive fragments and/or debris<br><br>* Can occur thousands of meters from the explosion [[13]](/library/REblvv)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Penetrating chest trauma</u><br><br>* <u>Penetrating abdominal trauma</u><br><br>* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u><br><br>* <u>Fractures</u><br><br>* <u>Amputations</u><br><br>* <u>Dislocations</u><br><br>* <u>Soft tissue</u> injury<br><br><br> |
| Tertiary blast injury | <br>* Trauma (typically <u>blunt trauma</u>) caused by:<br><br>* Displacement of the victim<br><br>* Structural collapse<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Blunt head injury</u><br><br>* <u>Blunt chest trauma</u><br><br>* <u>Blunt abdominal trauma</u><br><br>* <u>Crush injury</u><br><br>* <u>Compartment syndrome</u><br><br>* Traumatic <u>asphyxia</u><br><br>* <u>Fractures</u><br><br><br> |
| Quaternary blast injury | <br><br>* Explosion-related injury or disease caused by other mechanisms (e.g. heat, toxins)<br><br>* Includes exacerbation of chronic illnesses<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Thermal injury</u><br><br>* <u>Inhalation injury</u><br><br>* <u>Acute radiation injury</u><br><br>* <u>Carbon monoxide toxicity</u><br><br>* <u>Cyanide</u> toxicity<br><br>* <u>Organophosphate</u> toxicity<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Most injuries following an explosion result from blunt or <u>penetrating trauma</u> and are, therefore, secondary and/or <u>tertiary blast injuries</u>. [[15]](/library/9cWNe40)




### Approach to management [[11]](/library/fv1kzi0)[[16]](/library/j91_MQ0)




* In a combat setting, follow recommendations for tactical combat casualty care.

* Consider possible radiation and/or toxin exposure.

* Don appropriate <u>personal protective equipment</u>.

* <u>Body surface decontamination</u> of the patient may be indicated.

* Follow the <u>ATLS algorithm</u> for the initial <u>management of trauma patients</u>.

* <u>Primary survey</u>, including immediate <u>hemorrhage control</u>

* <u>Secondary survey</u>, including <u>otoscopic exam</u> to rule out <u>TM rupture</u>

* Maintain a high level of suspicion for <u>primary blast injuries</u>.

* Treat specific injuries according to protocol.

* Consider all wounds contaminated and provide <u>antibiotics for acute open wounds</u>. [[17]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Monitor extremity injuries for <u>acute compartment syndrome</u>.





> [!TIP]
> The management of most <u>blast injuries</u> is similar to the <u>management of traumatic injuries</u> from other causes.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Primary blast injuries</u> may not be immediately apparent. Maintain a high level of suspicion, especially in individuals found near the blast epicenter or in a confined space.




### <u>Primary blast injury</u> syndromes [[11]](/library/fv1kzi0)[[13]](/library/REblvv)[[14]](/library/gv1Fzi0)




#### Blast-induced otologic injury




* Definition: audiovestibular damage resulting from a <u>primary blast injury</u> to <u>the ear</u>

* Injuries: <u>tympanic membrane rupture</u> (most common <u>primary blast injury</u>) , <u>hearing loss</u>, <u>tinnitus</u>, <u>ear</u> <u>pain</u>, <u>vertigo</u>

* Management

* Screen patients with <u>otoscopy</u> in the acute setting and obtain <u>audiometry</u> when it is feasible.

* Consult otolaryngology for all patients with concerning findings.





![Ruptured tympanic membrane](media/l53kobjh1lanwse2ei9wi85j.jpg)

Ruptured tympanic membrane




#### Blast lung injury [[12]](/library/hv1c-i0)




* Definition: <u>pulmonary barotrauma</u> resulting from <u>primary blast injury</u> to the <u>lung</u>

* Injuries: pulmonary hemorrhage, <u>pulmonary edema</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>hemothorax</u>, and/or <u>arterial air embolism</u>

* Management: Consider <u>lung</u> imaging (e.g., <u>CXR</u>, chest CT, <u>lung</u> <u>ultrasound</u>) and early specialist consultation in patients with respiratory symptoms and those at high risk of <u>blast lung injury</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Blast lung</u> is the most common cause of fatality among those who survive the initial explosion. [[14]](/library/gv1Fzi0)




#### Blast-induced neurotrauma (BINT) [[18]](/library/B91zpQ0)[[19]](/library/U1WbT40)




* Definition: a type of <u>traumatic brain injury</u> resulting from direct <u>primary blast injury</u> of the <u>CNS</u>  [[20]](/library/AcWRU40)

* Clinical features: <u>signs of mild traumatic brain injury</u> (<u>mTBI</u>)

* Diagnostics: Consider <u>criteria for neuroimaging in mTBI</u> to rule out <u>blunt head injuries</u> and <u>penetrating brain injuries</u>. [[21]](/library/wmXh3A)

* Management: See “<u>Treatment of mTBI</u>.”





#### Blast-induced ocular trauma




* Definition: ocular damage resulting from a direct <u>primary blast injury</u> to the <u>eye</u>

* Injuries: globe rupture, <u>conjunctival</u> hemorrhage , <u>hyphema</u>  , retinitis, and/or <u>orbital fractures</u>

* Management

* Maintain a low threshold for urgent ophthalmologic consultation.

* See “<u>Traumatic eye injuries</u>.”





![Subconjunctival hemorrhage](media/yw87fz5m6sebcxw8cmfea2t3.jpg)

Subconjunctival hemorrhage

![Hyphema](media/m2pd705tbelwf96adhpstrw2.jpg)

Hyphema




#### Blast-induced abdominal injury




* Definition: <u>primary blast injury</u> to the intraabdominal organs

* Injuries: <u>gastrointestinal perforation</u>, <u>gastrointestinal bleeding</u>, and/or solid organ <u>laceration</u> or rupture

* Management

* Obtain imaging (e.g., <u>FAST scan</u>, abdominal CT) for patients with abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>peritoneal signs</u>, or <u>signs of GI bleeding</u>.

* See “<u>Approach to blunt abdominal trauma</u>,” “<u>Treatment of gastrointestinal perforation</u>,” and “<u>Initial management of an overt GI bleed</u>.”





#### Cardiovascular primary blast injuries




* Blast-induced <u>vasovagal response</u>: <u>bradycardia</u> and <u>hypotension</u> lasting minutes to hours

* Other (less common): <u>cardiac contusion</u>, <u>coronary artery</u> <u>air embolism</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>asystole</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> Treatment-resistant <u>hemorrhagic shock</u> may indicate an underlying <u>cardiovascular primary blast injury</u>. [[14]](/library/gv1Fzi0)
